newsitem.title: UK: Dlr dips in thin conditions, keeps wary eye on Dow.
newsitem.headline: Dlr dips in thin conditions, keeps wary eye on Dow.

text.p: The dollar closed lower in European trading, dragged down by squaring of long positions and a sharp fall of stocks in early U.S. trade, dealers said.

Selling pressure on the dollar was exacerbated by thin trading and the wait-and-see attitude many players adopted ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Tuesday. "In a market like that a few big trades can have quite a big effect, so the dollar came under a bit of pressure this afternoon," said Pat Magill, head of the corporate desk at Daiwa Europe in London.
At 1449 the dollar was at 1.5125/30 marks and 109.80/85 yen compared with 1.5140/47 and 109.77/82 in late Europe on Friday.

Squaring of longs in dollar/Swiss spilled over into dollar/mark but dealers said the dollar was well supported against both the Swiss franc and the mark by bids around 1.5120 marks and in the mid-1.23 Swiss franc area.

A recovery of the mark on its crosses also undermined the dollar, traders said. The mark bounced off lows hit in early trading after last weekend's meeting of European finance ministers saw broad consensus on the starting data for EMU in 1999, the stability pact and a post-EMU exchange rate mechanism.
Dealers noted that concern about political instability in Russia amid renewed fears about the health of President Boris Yeltsin supported the Swiss franc but the impact was marginal.
A rise of 25 basis points in the Fed funds target rate at the FOMC meeting is well priced into the dollar, analysts said.

"After all the speculation regarding the outcome of the meeting a 25 basis points tightening of the Fed funds rate would come as something of an anti-climax," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered.
Such a move would keep dollar bears at bay, while inaction might prompt a retracement of some of the recent dollar gains.

If the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) fails to sanction a rise at Tuesday's meeting, the dollar would be at risk of weakening as some of the long positions built up in the run-up to the meeting would be unwound, traders said.
Inaction would fuel suspicion politics were influencing monetary policy before general elections in November. In addition, hawkish forces, worried about inflation, would take fright.
A larger-than-expected rise could initially give the dollar upside momentum, but some also argued that it might backfire since the market might consider it as a panic move by the Fed.

A poll conducted by Reuters last week showed opinion remains divided. A slim majority of economists polled, 17 of 30, believed the Fed would opt to raise short-term rates. All but one of those analysts expected a small increase of one-quarter percentage point.
